reading.rtitle: A Second Chance, Close to Home
paras: Ten years ago, doctors in Brazil couldn't offer CAR-T therapy. It was already a breakthrough in the United States, but patients here couldn't get it. Only a few families were able to pay for a trip abroad and stay there for months. Most patients couldn't afford it.

Marina is a teacher from Recife. Three years ago, she had lymphoma, and the first two treatments didn't work. "I couldn't walk to the corner. I couldn't work, and I couldn't play with my son," she says.

Then a cancer hospital in Sao Paulo started a CAR-T program, and the hospital committee approved her case. Marina was able to do the therapy in Brazil, near her family. There were side effects in the first two weeks, but the team could control them.

Today, Marina can walk, work and play with her son again. She recovered, and she is back at school. The survival rate for patients like her is better now, but access is still a problem: many hospitals can't offer the therapy yet. "I was lucky," Marina says. "I hope that in five years every patient will be able to get it."
reading.source: A short story written for this lesson, based on what many patients live when a new cancer therapy arrives in their country.

listenings.text: Good morning, everyone. My name is Doctor Paulo Lima, and I work with CAR-T therapy here in Sao Paulo. Let me tell you why this therapy is a breakthrough. Some patients with blood cancer try two or three treatments, and nothing works. Ten years ago, we couldn't do much for them. Now we can take the patient's own cells, change them in a lab, and put them back. The process takes about four weeks. There can be side effects, so the patient has to stay near the hospital for a month. Last year, we were able to treat forty patients, and most of them recovered well. Our next step is access. In a few years, I hope patients from all over Brazil will be able to get this therapy close to home.

Hi Fernando, it's Sarah. I read your access report on the plane, and I have one big question for our call on Monday. In the United States, many patients can get CAR-T, but some families can't afford the trip and the month near the hospital. Last year, one of our partner hospitals in Texas was able to solve this with a small apartment program. The hospital pays for an apartment, and the family can stay together. Could your network do something like that? I couldn't find it in your report. Maybe it is a good idea for your 2028 goal. Let's talk about it on Monday. Bye!
